evidence.section_title: Finally, it became too much – experiences and reflections in the aftermath of attempted suicide
evidence.quote: Nine of the participants had experienced one or more suicide attempts. One person had been prevented in the attempt, by hospitalization in an emergency ward.

The purpose of this study was to explore experiences following suicide crises or recent suicide attempts. The research question was 'What thoughts do suicidal patients have about the crisis they have experienced?'

[/page/1/Text/13] The interview subject must (i) have been considered seriously suicidal, but in the event of a suicide attempt, the interview should take place no earlier than 2 weeks afterwards, (ii) not be psychotic, (iii) be able to verbalize his/her experiences and (iv) have access to a therapist at least 2 weeks after the interview. The participants consisted of four women, aged from 21 to 45 years, and six men, aged from 25 to 52 years. Nine had made suicidal attempts prior to the interview, and one of them had tried four times during the previous month. Four persons had made one or more attempts in the past. Suicide was attempted by pills or substances. Five persons told about consumption of alcohol in advance of, or while taking, the pills. One person interviewed had not attempted suicide, but was prevented from carrying out a carefully planned suicide only by being involuntarily hospitalized.

evidence.section_title: Finally, it became too much – experiences and reflections in the aftermath of attempted suicide
evidence.quote: Data were collected using qualitative research interviews.
[/page/1/Text/13] Ten people participated in the study after having been informed and requested by specialists in psychology at three places of emergency psychiatry and by crisis resolution teams.
Research interviews were used (26, 27) to collect data about the experiences and reflections of the participants relating to being suicidal.

evidence.section_title: Finally, it became too much – experiences and reflections in the aftermath of attempted suicide
evidence.quote: Results obtained through a thematic analysis of six phases revealed five themes to be central: (i) Losing touch with the world, (ii) Relationship between the suicidal accident and life history, (iii) Struggling for death and life (iv) An open door as consolation and (v) Feeling shame and guilt. Being suicidal seems like a struggle in solitude, between longing to escape from suffering through death and longing for love, safety and dignity in life. Suicidal accidents happen when suffering becomes intolerable. Suicide rarely occurs without a struggle and consideration of moral conflicts. The thought of suicide can provide consolation and comfort to go on living. Shame seems to appear when a person cannot cope with her/his own life, and because of failed attempts, while guilt seems related to hurting other people.

The metaphors that the interviewees use to describe their condition prior to the suicide attempt often relate to being alone in darkness. Expressions were noted, such as 'having been down in the basement and being dragged down by one thing or another', as well as references to an uncontrollable force, 'to lie below the ice and not be able to get up' and to being in a dark room 'where I cannot find the door; don't find the light switch'. Most tell about a condition where the darkness gradually increased and the decision to commit suicide emerged, 'I had simply given up'. For some, the decision was more abrupt, as a consequence of 'an immense feeling of hopelessness'. One interviewee describes his own condition as 'being inside a black cardboard box' and 'being surrounded by a totally black fog'. The person described how 'the bubble burst' when his condition changed from being 'completely up in cloud to turn into black' within 3 days, where the decision, 'I can't bear this', was taken. Also, another interviewee compares the condition with being in a black bubble: It's like I'm sitting inside a tiny bubble, a black bubble, that I'm the only one in there and no one else is able to get into it, and which I cannot get out of. When I'm so far down, everything is so black and dark that nothing can affect on you from the outside, because you enter a kind of psychosis. Several persons describe their longing for someone who is able to see, listen and understand. 'In my life I've never really had anyone who has been listening much', as one person said. 'It feels despairing not to be believed when you try to tell others about your depression'. To fight while suffering in solitude can be exhausting. The longing for someone to lean on, figuratively speaking, someone who can bring hope into periods when life is experienced without any flashes is understood as an essential element before, during and after the suicide crisis. Is it so that the deepest suffering experienced by the suicidal person is that of not being confirmed in his lonely struggle for life?

evidence.section_title: Relationship between the suicidal accident and life history
evidence.quote: [page/3/Text/6] Throughout the stories, vulnerability, as well as the courage and strength to carry different loads over time, becomes visible. Eight of the 10 interview subjects tell of events and conditions in early stages of their life, which have contributed to forming their attitudes to themselves and to life in general. 'That was presumably in the beginning, the problems started; it is something about my self-esteem. I have still some of these thoughts, that it is my fault', as one of the interviewees said. Several talked about how incidents and feelings have been 'not-themes' in their life, as loss and grief, like this guy: [page/3/Text/8] Interview subjects reflect on how their inter-relational problems and breaks with important people in their lives, substance abuse, physical injuries and psychological problems, excessive workload, and loss of meaningful tasks in everyday life are affecting their mental health and spirit. One interviewee tells about rape and another about prostitution and how this has affected their self-image. Several said that the idea of suicide came as early as in childhood or in their teen years and was triggered by bullying, identity problems and losses through their parents' divorce, or death of a mother, as in this case: 'I can remember the anxiety, and then the blues started at 9–10 years of age and, as a consequence, I suppose, these thoughts about suicide came creeping in over the teens'.

Statements such as 'I had decided to die' could illustrate the interviewees' determination prior to the suicide attempt. Other statements, such as: 'If I had had more pills I would have taken more' and 'If I had had weapons available that night a month ago, I wouldn't have been alive today', seem to be expressions of a strong desire and willingness to die. The reflection: 'Did I have luck or bad luck?' seems to illustrate that the interviewees do not immediately feel joy of having survived. To many, it seems like a coincidence that they were found or managed to report the overdose in time, either to a friend or to the emergency ward, while one interviewee says: 'I really just wanted to get help'. Some of the interviewees were frightened by their own actions, especially by 'the courage part'. Two male interviewees said, however, that now they felt more confident that they would be able to carry out an eventual suicide, and one of them said that his fear of death was less. A woman said: 'I think everything is easier if you've done it once, then you can do it several times. I hope not, but I'm afraid I can do it' (i.e. to accomplish a new suicide attempt). As I swallowed the sleeping pills down with red wine, I was thinking, ah, now it'll be over. Then the feeling came, that you get a little happy, because you know somehow that now the race is run, now you're finished... And then, when I woke up next morning and realized that I had not made it I got really pissed off... But then I realized that I had taken too little, so I stumbled back home, and then I took something I had left in another box... I thought that now it's certainly over, and then the same feeling came again, when I realized that it started to work, it was such a relief to know that now at least you should make it. Then I woke up, as my wife was standing there, shaking me violently, shaking life back into my body, I can remember being very annoyed. I considered very carefully, then I was beginning to be affected by the pills already, as I was lying in bed and had been chewing pills for several hours, and had counted all the pills I had and thought that I'll manage to make it with these. But then I remembered clearly from last time that, I woke up again 2 ½ years ago thinking: Oh, my God, if I fail again this time, it must not happen, if I decide to die, then I must die, somehow. But I was very determined that I should do it. I cried a lot while I was in my room and I wrote a farewell letter, this time as well (to my grown up children and other close relatives), just a short note. And there I was sitting in the evening, counting pills, with a bunch in each hand, shall – shall not, shall – shall not, but something held me back. The interviewees expressed some of the considerations preceding the suicide attempt. Responsibility for family members was especially emphasized as difficult. Also, responsibility for their own lives, to complete projects in life, such as a vocational training, had to be weighed against the desire to avoid suffering. One of the interviewees described the conflict involved in the suicide decision, as 'a clear spirit being present all the time, that I want to make it an end and at the same time I can see the value of living'. Suicide is not regarded as an easy decision and solution, but as an expression of a struggle between the desire for relief from suffering and a longing for life, where the suffering gets the upper hand.

Two of the interviewees reflect upon 'having an open door, an option available'; how the thought of being able to put an end to one's suffering if it should become unbearable, is comforting and makes it possible to endure suffering. Another tells of how desperation increased when he was involuntarily hospitalized after the therapist became aware of his suicide plan. Hospitalization restricts access to medications and other methods and also to personal freedom. As one interviewee puts it: There are a few things I just have to keep for myself, well,... and I must have a possibility, I must have an exit which is available. The interviewee explains why he, at the present time, could not tell the staff about his razor blades: 'in a good period, when things work out well for me, when, when I feel I have control over my life, it's in this situation I would be able to see my therapist and talk about this'. An interviewee, who had carried out four suicide attempts in a month, describes the process from the perspective of suicide as relief and consolation to an awareness that suicide was something that could become an actuality: I was never as comfortable as when I first had taken the decision. For about a fortnight or so I just played with the idea, but viewed in retrospect, it wasn't only a play with the idea, but more of a consciousness that I was going to do it in a few weeks. And just that, to lose perspective on what's going to happen, you cannot enjoy anything, everything is just completely indifferent. You play with the thought pretty often (the thought of suicide), and then it's fortified and becomes a kind of obsession, like when you put down a seed that grows and finally overshadows everything, and when the thought is settled, then of course you're afraid to reveal what you've been playing with in your mind... I think it may be difficult for a client to speak up after the thought has changed from being such a comfort, like a dream, to become something like the solution. Freedom and responsibility also entail conflict. The certainty of having control over own life can provide a comfort when suffering feels unbearable. The consolation may change to become an obsession with suicide that overshadows everything and where comfort appears as the solution. Could it be so that the destructive will decide, not the person himself, that I'm doing something I don't want, after all?

[page/5/Text/9] The theme is understood as longing for being understood and loved (9–12), which can account for a risk of suicide (30). [page/5/Text/10] Extensive research has shown that hopelessness is the link between depression and increased risk of suicide (34). [page/5/Text/10] Longings and desires are about the future and bring hope for something or someone who can help. Hope is understood as relational (33). [page/5/Text/11] According to Lindstrom, allowing oneself to be touched by the other's longing might be a gateway to breaking through the 'shimmer of loneliness' (10) and to relieving life suffering (16, 17). [page/5/Text/12] Mental illness is considered a major factor in most suicides and suicide attempts (1, 3, 36). [page/5/Text/13] Isolation provides more space and 'nutrition' for suicidal thoughts, and in the data, it is compared to 'a seed that grows and overshadows everything'. [page/6/Text/2] In this struggle, this study showed a reflection about moral responsibility towards himself and especially towards related persons, as also reported by Tzeng (14). [page/6/Text/3] Suicidality functions as a survival strategy, and as a way of problem solving (41), until what was experienced as comforting becomes a threat, and suicide then appears to be the solution. [page/6/Text/4] In this study, shame and guilt are associated with failure because the persons neither cope with own life nor are they being successful with the suicidal attempt. [page/6/Text/5] On the other hand, a respectful attitude from professional helpers contributes to reduce shame (12– 14, 46).

Risk: "Suicide attempts can be understood as an action in the aftermath of a struggle in solitude, between longing for relief from suffering through death and longing for love, safety and dignity in life. Suicide accidents came into being after a short or long process of unbearable and usually long-lasting suffering. The thought of suicide as a way out not only can give help to endure suffering but can also be a threat to own life. Suicidal persons undergo moral deliberations, which is in contradiction to many people's view of suicide as a selfish act. Shame and guilt appeared as feelings that were fortified by negative attitudes from the surrounding community." Recovery: "Some of the health professionals' challenges were to reach a relationship with the suicidal person before the barrier became total, which requires engagement, time and space." "This means more descriptions about suicidal thoughts and feelings, which could help communicating about life and death, shame, guilt, loneliness, desire and longing, in a way that gives hope for life."
